title: Magazine Depth Affordability Is a Choice | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z partner Alex Oliver argues US munitions magazine depth is unaffordable only because the Pentagon allocates 97% of its munitions plan to legacy rounds costing $2-70 million each, when new entrants like Anduril, Castelion and Covenant field comparable strike effects for $300,000-$700,000 using automotive, consumer-electronics and civil-aviation supply chains funded by private capital. With the FY27 NDAA authorizing a record $1.15 trillion topline, he contends money, demand signal and multiyear authorities all now exist, so allocation — not budget — is the binding constraint. Interceptors remain the unsolved frontier, with CBO pricing Golden Dome at $1.2 trillion over twenty years if built with today's cost structure.

insights.claim: The Pentagon's Munitions Acceleration Council plan assigns 97 percent of munitions funding to legacy munitions and less than three percent to new entrants building lower-cost products with modernized design and manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: The 3% slice is the addressable budget wedge for defense-tech new entrants today; any policy shift toward low-cost munitions expands their TAM by an order of magnitude off a tiny base.
insights.quote: less than three percent
insights.locator: According to Wicker's hearing

insights.claim: Because the Pentagon already has the money, the demand signal and the multiyear procurement authorities it spent the 2010s saying it lacked, allocation is the only remaining decision that determines magazine depth.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Watch allocation line items, not toplines — incremental defense budget growth no longer reads through automatically to primes if the mix shifts.
insights.quote: The department spent the 2010s explaining that it lacked the money, the demand signal, and the authorities to buy munitions at scale. As of this budget, it has all three.
insights.locator: 5. Allocation Is the Only Decision Left

insights.claim: Under a simplified $100 munitions budget with legacy rounds at $1 and new entrants at ten cents, the current 97-to-3 split fields roughly 73 legacy rounds plus 30 new-entrant rounds, whereas a 1:3 legacy-to-cheap mix would buy 61 legacy plus 180 new-entrant missiles.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A simple Pareto-frontier framing that reframes procurement debates as a portfolio allocation problem rather than a budget-size problem.
insights.quote: Every way of splitting the $100 lands somewhere on the Pareto frontier line, and the current plan's chosen point sits in its far upper-left corner.
insights.locator: Buying Tradeoffs: Simplified

insights.claim: The FY27 NDAA cleared by the Senate Armed Services Committee authorizes $1.15 trillion for national defense, the largest topline in history, with the administration requesting a 188 percent increase in missile procurement and the Munitions Acceleration Council priority list exceeding $47 billion.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A 188% jump in missile procurement demand plus a $47 billion priority list sets the size of the pool that both primes and startups are competing to capture.
insights.quote: authorizes $1.15 trillion for national defense, the largest topline in history
insights.locator: 5. Allocation Is the Only Decision Left

insights.claim: The Senate Armed Services Committee markup advanced 18-9 on June 11 requires acceleration of low-cost munitions adoption in eight critical categories, authorizes multiyear munitions procurement, and mandates second sources for solid rocket motors.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A bipartisan 18-9 vote signals real legislative momentum behind the low-cost munitions thesis, creating a concrete catalyst calendar for new entrants.
insights.locator: The committee, to its credit, has proposed a remedy

insights.claim: Liquid propulsion technologies, as a complement to solid rocket motors, are presented as the only way to truly unstick the solid-rocket-motor bottleneck, beyond simply mandating second sources.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A non-consensus technology bet: liquid-propulsion munitions startups could bypass the SRM bottleneck that constrains every legacy line.
insights.quote: though we believe liquid propulsion technologies as a complement to solid motors are the only way to truly unstick this logjam
insights.locator: The committee, to its credit, has proposed a remedy

insights.claim: A Tomahawk costs about $2-4 million and LRASM $3.2 million, while hypersonics like the Army's Dark Eagle and the Navy's Conventional Prompt Strike cost between $41 million and $70 million per missile.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: These per-round prices are the cost umbrella new entrants price under; they set the ceiling for how much margin a low-cost challenger can capture.
insights.locator: 2. The Cost of a Legacy Magazine

insights.claim: Defensive interceptors price even higher than strike weapons: PAC-3 MSE at $3.9 million, a THAAD round at $12-22 million, and an SM-3 Block IIA at $28 million and up.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Interceptor economics are the worst in the magazine and the least disrupted, making them the largest unaddressed cost-reduction opportunity.
insights.locator: The defensive interceptors are also steep

insights.claim: Fielding even four thousand LRASM-class anti-ship weapons — described as modest for a Taiwan scenario — costs $13 billion at current prices against a production line throughput that only just reached about 1,100 missiles a year shared with JASSM.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Quantifies the arithmetic impossibility of buying deterrence-sized depth at legacy prices, which is the core investment case for low-cost alternatives.
insights.quote: Even the largest defense topline in American history cannot procure deterrence-sized depth at seven and eight figures a round.
insights.locator: The publicly conducted wargames call for thousands

insights.claim: The published flyaway price of a legacy munition understates its true cost because government-funded RDT&E adds roughly 25% of lifecycle cost, widening the legacy-to-new-entrant gap from five-to-ten times to potentially twelve-to-fifteen times.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Standard cost comparisons systematically flatter incumbents; adjusting for government-funded R&D roughly doubles the apparent advantage of privately developed rounds.
insights.quote: In Fiscal Year 2025, the Pentagon's missile and munitions request ran about two-thirds procurement to one-third research and development
insights.locator: So each incremental legacy missile costs

insights.claim: Government buying behavior itself inflates unit cost, as shown when the Army bought only 23 JAGM missiles in FY25 and the unit price hit $360,000 against a program-life average of $212,000.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Order-size volatility is a hidden cost driver; multiyear procurement authority is therefore a direct margin and price lever, not just a convenience.
insights.quote: Jittery buying is itself part of what makes munitions expensive.
insights.locator: The government's capricious buying decisions

themes.theme: New Entrant Price Points and Contracts

insights.claim: Commercially built strike weapons such as Covenant's Anthem and Anduril's Barracuda family cost about one-fifth to one-tenth of a Tomahawk's $2-4 million.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Establishes the 5-10x cost delta that underpins the entire allocation argument and the valuation case for these private companies.
insights.locator: Take cruise missiles as example A

insights.claim: Lockheed Martin's PrSM Increment 1, initially priced at $2.7 million and now $1.7 million with scale, is less performant than Castelion's Hypersonic Blackbeard GL entering at under $500,000.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A direct like-for-like where the startup beats the incumbent on both price and performance — the clearest disruption signal in the article.
insights.locator: Then examine close and short range ballistic missiles as example B

insights.claim: Castelion's Blackbeard has a signed framework for 500 or more missiles per year and a Navy program of record planning 4,510 rounds across FY27-31.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Converts the low-cost thesis from concept to contracted revenue with a five-year visible order book.
insights.locator: On the strike side, the inexpensive, effective option

insights.claim: The Air Force's Family of Affordable Mass Munitions plans nearly 28,000 weapons for $12.6 billion, with production starting in September 2026.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Implies roughly $450,000 per round at genuine scale, validating that affordable mass is now a funded program of record rather than a proposal.
insights.locator: The Air Force's Family of Affordable Mass Munitions

insights.claim: Anduril will supply the Army at least 3,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500Ms with first deliveries in mid-2027.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A dated delivery milestone to track as a proof point for whether new entrants can actually hit rate production.
insights.locator: Anduril will supply the Army

insights.claim: Hard cost ceilings are being written into new programs, with the Navy's MACE capping its hypersonic round at $300,000, the Air Force's affordable-mass cruise missile line at about $400,000, and several companies now competing in the $300,000-to-$600,000 band.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Price ceilings plus multiple bidders mean margin compression is designed into this market from the start — volume, not price, is where returns come from.
insights.locator: The new programs are built around competition

insights.claim: The deterrent quality of a munitions magazine is a function of both inventory on hand and the capacity to produce more, with production carrying vastly more weight in a rational adversary's calculation than inventory alone.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Reframes deterrence value toward warm production lines, favoring companies that own scalable factories over those holding stockpile contracts.
insights.quote: Production carries vastly more weight in any rational actor's calculation than inventory alone.
insights.locator: At its core, the deterrent quality of our magazine

insights.claim: Across the first thirty-nine days of Operation Epic Fury the Navy fired more than 1,000 Tomahawks from a stockpile of roughly 3,100, the Air Force expended about 80 percent of its JASSM-ER inventory, and Patriot batteries fired 943 interceptors in the first four days — about eighteen months of output at current throughput.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A live demonstration that a regional campaign can drain a third of a flagship stockpile in weeks — the strongest empirical driver of replenishment demand.
insights.locator: Across the first thirty-nine days of Operation Epic Fury

insights.claim: Rebuilding the inventories consumed by Operation Epic Fury — Tomahawk, JASSM, Patriot, THAAD, SM-2 and SM-6 — takes eight to fourteen years at historical production rates.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: An 8-14 year replenishment horizon implies a decade-long revenue tailwind for munitions capacity regardless of which supplier class wins.
insights.quote: at historical production rates, replacing major-program inventories takes eight to fourteen years
insights.locator: Operation Epic Fury consumed munition stockpiles

insights.claim: A bipartisan commission chartered by Congress to review defense strategy stated flatly that the defense industrial base is unable to meet U.S. and allied munitions needs, and widely cited wargames concluded the U.S. would run out of preferred munitions in the early days with resupply not an option.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Official consensus on industrial base inadequacy is the political precondition for the allocation shift this article advocates.
insights.quote: the U.S. will run out of preferred munitions in the early days
insights.locator: 1. Adversaries Count Rounds

themes.theme: Cost Per Effect Over Cost Per Round

insights.claim: The correct metric is cost per effect rather than raw munition capability, and reframing targeting this way skews the round of choice overwhelmingly toward the cheaper option while preserving exquisite legacy rounds for hardened, heavily defended targets.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A doctrine shift toward cost-per-effect would structurally reallocate volume from primes to low-cost producers without eliminating legacy demand entirely.
insights.quote: Simply put, new entrant rounds will cover the bulk of targets based on the cost per effect model.
insights.locator: Analysts have warned against a race to the bottom

insights.claim: Most of a modern target set — trucks, radars, small ships, drones, buildings, massed infantry — does not require a $3 million munition, and equating a munition's cost with its capability has been a longstanding error.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Establishes that the majority of target volume is addressable by cheap rounds, defining the revenue pool new entrants can take.
insights.quote: we have equated the cost of a munition with the capability of that munition.
insights.locator: 3. Measure the Cost of Effects

insights.claim: The real lesson of $4 million Patriots intercepting $20,000 drones in Epic Fury is not a bad exchange ratio but a magazine without optionality, because the expensive interceptor was the only answer in inventory.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Reframes the cost-exchange debate as a product-portfolio gap, pointing demand toward a missing tier of cheap interceptors.
insights.quote: every cheap drone got the $4 million Patriot because that was the only answer in inventory
insights.locator: The now infamous cost-exchange stat

insights.claim: Low-cost cruise missiles such as Barracuda-500, RAACM-ER and Covenant's Anthem now compete with Tomahawk on range, quality and increasingly warhead size, which does not make Tomahawk obsolete but enables heterogeneous salvos from multiple directions that improve air defense penetration.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Mixed-tier salvos are the operational rationale for buying both, implying coexistence rather than outright displacement of incumbents.
insights.locator: But the low-cost class now includes cruise missiles

insights.claim: The critique that mass production should focus on ordnance rather than drones is partly conceded, since the Pacific's brutal distances render prolific quadcopters incapable of relevant operational reach and force a return to more expensive long-range systems with rocket motors and sophisticated guidance.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Cheap FPV-style drone plays do not translate to the Pacific; the investable low-cost category there is long-range cruise and ballistic munitions.
insights.quote: distance forces you back toward more expensive, long-range systems with rocket motors and sophisticated guidance
insights.locator: Some critics argue that mass production

insights.claim: A CSIS study found that between 2022 and 2024 Russia fired nearly four one-way attack UAVs for every costlier cruise or ballistic missile launched at Ukraine, a ratio that widened to roughly 1:10 as Shahed production scaled in late 2024.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: An empirical benchmark from a peer military for what a modern magazine mix looks like, used as a directional guidepost rather than an ideal target.
insights.locator: A CSIS study showed that between 2022 and 2024

insights.claim: Affordable mass is best defined as a property of the production system rather than the price tag — the condition in which a force replaces munitions as fast as it expends them.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Diligence should center on throughput and reliability, not sticker price, since a cheap unreliable round is not actually cheap.
insights.quote: a $200K weapon with half the reliability is really a $400K solution
insights.locator: 4. The Factory Is the Product

insights.claim: Anduril's Barracuda assembles in about 30 labor-hours from roughly 70 percent commercial components, drawing on small-aviation and automotive supply chains rather than aerospace sub-tiers.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: 30 labor-hours and 70% commercial content is the concrete manufacturing benchmark against which rival munitions startups should be measured.
insights.locator: By that standard, the new class was designed

insights.claim: The claim that the two-year missile build time cannot be compressed by money applies only to old-style missiles that are custom-designed, single-sourced and hand-assembled by high-skill technicians, not to munitions built from plentiful automotive, consumer electronics and civil aviation supply chains on privately funded lines built ahead of need.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: If correct, new entrants can convert appropriations into delivered rounds far faster than incumbents, which is the decisive competitive variable in a surge.
insights.quote: the problem today isn't money; it's time
insights.locator: Critics counter that at this point

insights.claim: Scaling legacy lines is happening but is expensive and taxpayer-funded, with PAC-3 MSE going from about 600 interceptors a year toward 2,000 under a seven-year framework, THAAD from 96 toward 400, and SM-6 from 125 toward more than 500.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Concrete multi-year capacity expansion targets for incumbent interceptor lines, funded by government capex rather than private balance sheets.
insights.quote: Unfortunately, the American people are going to have to shoulder much of the burden for those capex projects.
insights.locator: It's harder and more expensive to scale the legacy production lines

insights.claim: Unreliable government demand is the greatest obstacle to warm production capacity, with one study of two decades of munitions budgets finding funding swinging more than 50 percent year-over-year across eighty programs.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: 50%+ annual budget volatility explains why primes will not build capacity on spec and why privately funded capacity is a genuine differentiator.
insights.locator: The greatest challenge to maintaining warm production capacity

insights.claim: When the Deputy Secretary of War began calling missile-industry CEOs weekly to push for increased output, executives gave the same answer they have given for a decade — that the targets are not realistic without contracts to finance them.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Political pressure alone will not move incumbent output; only contract structure does, which is precisely the gap private capital fills.

insights.claim: Augustine's Law cost inflation is a real risk for advertised-as-affordable programs, as shown by the Collaborative Combat Aircraft exceeding its $3 million target to reach $25-30 million, but that dynamic describes requirements floating free under cost-plus contracts with a monopoly supplier rather than fixed-price competitive programs.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: The 10x CCA overrun is the bear case for low-cost munitions; contract structure (fixed price, multiple vendors, hard ceilings) is the variable to monitor for whether it repeats.
insights.locator: There is concern that new products advertised as affordable

insights.claim: Lower-cost air defense interceptors are the greatest area of need and require a Manhattan Project-type effort to develop affordable alternatives to Patriot, THAAD and the Standard Missile series.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Flags the next investable wave after strike munitions, with political air cover already articulated at the committee chairman level.
insights.quote: perhaps, our greatest area of need
insights.locator: Air Defense Is Next…

insights.claim: CBO puts the Golden Dome homeland-defense architecture at $1.2 trillion over twenty years if built with today's interceptor cost structure, far above the administration's proposed budget, with General Guetlein emphatic that the country cannot be bankrupted to build it.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: The gap between a $1.2 trillion estimate and a fraction-of-that budget is the forcing function that will pull cheap interceptor technology into procurement.
insights.locator: CBO puts the Golden Dome homeland-defense architecture

insights.claim: Whether interceptors can follow strike weapons down the cost curve remains an open question because the engineering problem is harder and no one has demonstrated the answer yet.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: An explicit admission of unproven technical risk — the single biggest uncertainty in the affordable-mass thesis and in Golden Dome economics.
insights.quote: the engineering problem is harder, and no one has demonstrated the answer yet
insights.locator: Whether interceptors can follow strike weapons

insights.claim: US sovereign demand outpacing supply has left allies and partners facing five- to seven-year backlogs for some traditional munitions, driving them toward non-US component manufacturers to bridge the gap.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: A concrete market-share leakage risk for US primes and an opening for European and other non-US munitions suppliers.
insights.quote: are now turning to non-US component manufacturers to bridge the gap
insights.locator: The fact that our sovereign demand outpaces supply

insights.claim: A $300,000 missile built from commercial components is one an ally can actually afford in quantity and, where policy allows, license and co-produce, with the FY27 bill directing a U.S.-German co-production program and war-reserve stockpile authority for Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Low-cost designs unlock an export and co-production channel that legacy price points close off, expanding the addressable market beyond US budgets.
insights.locator: A $300,000 missile built from commercial components

insights.claim: Superfluous munition capability should never be paid for by the taxpayer in a country carrying $30 trillion in debt, and the volume of effects a force can deliver and replace across a long fight is what actually influences adversary decision making.
insights.speaker: Alex Oliver
insights.so_what: Ties defense procurement reform to the fiscal constraint, suggesting budget pressure will reinforce rather than reverse the shift to cheap munitions.
insights.quote: But the American taxpayer should never be paying for superfluous capability. Certainly not in a world where we are $30 trillion in debt!
